newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr deadlocked, data a shock for GDP.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr deadlocked, data a shock for GDP.

text.p: The Australian dollar was little changed at the midsession having bobbed about in a tight 20-tick range as bids and offers were fairly evenly balanced.

Domestic data were again too mixed to offer much direction and anyway had been robbed of much of their significance by last week's rate cut. Nevertheless, a surprise 2.1 percent drop in business inventories made the RBA's move look a little more timely since it promised to knock a whopping 1.7 percentage points off GDP growth in the March quarter.
That meant annual growth would slow sharply in Q1, although analysts noted it improved the prospects for a bounce in Q2/Q3.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar had faded to US$0.7640/45 from an early US$0.7651/56 but was at least keeping its distance from the offshore low of US$0.7615.
It finished at US$0.7658/63 here Wednesday and had held to a US$0.7615/7675 range since Friday's 1-1/2 cent collapse.

On the crosses the currency lost further ground to the yen as Japanese bond rates continued heavenward, with the key 10-year JGB contract up 0.050 point today to 2.735 percent against 2.550 percent at the end of last week.
Just a month ago this bond had been yielding only 2.155 percent, so the rise had been vast and violent in JGB terms.

The surge reflected signs of genuine recovery in the Japanese economy which meant it was only a matter of time -- albeit months according to most analysts -- before the Bank of Japan lifted short term rates from their record low levels.

And while Japanese yields had been surging, domestic rates had fallen sharply in the wake of the Reserve Bank's rate cut making A$ assets less attractive, particularly against the US$, to Japanese investors.
The market could not even be sure if the RBA easing cycle had ended given the bank's confidence on inflation and readiness to go for growth as a remedy for high unemployment.
Today's weak inventory data held a mixed message for policy in that while it boded ill for gorwth in Q1, it promised to support a recovery in production as the year progressed.

The 2.1 percent fall was the first since the September quarter of 1993 and had analysts hastily revising down forecasts of Q1 GDP growth to below 1.0 percent. That meant annual growth was set to slow sharply from the 3.1 percent seen in Q4 -- 1.0 percent on the quarter would yield 2.4 percent on the year.
However, the rundown in stocks confirmed retail sales had been robust in the quarter and suggested industrial production would pick up in Q2/Q3 as inventory levels were re-built.
This natural pick-up could be expected to be supported by last week's policy easing thus raising the chance that growth might surprise on the upside in 1997/98.

Today's other release showed Australian exports performed strongly in April to swing the balance of goods and serviced into a surplus of A$300 million from a deficit of A$103 million in March. Goods exports rose eight percent while imports were flat on the month.
The data suggested the country's current account deficit was still some way from becoming a burden again and should support dollar sentiment at the margin.
The quarterly balance of payments data for Q1 are due Friday and will contain the first estimate of the current account deficit now that monthly figures have been dropped.
The local dollar stood at 88.24/34 yen from 88.80/90 late Wednesday and was down at 58.1 in trade weighted terms from a previous 58.3 finish.
